title: Word With the Odd Step Pattern
statement:
You get an array words of lowercase strings, all of the same length m. The step pattern of a word is the list of m − 1 gaps between neighbouring letters, measured in alphabet positions: for each j, word[j + 1] − word[j]. Gaps can be negative. For example, "bdc" has the pattern [2, −1].

All words share the same step pattern except exactly one. Return that word.

examples.why: Letters far apart can share a pattern: "zy", "ba" and "dc" all step [−1]. "ef" steps [+1].
"aa" and "bb" both step [0]. The odd word is the first one, so comparing everything against words[0] would flag the wrong word.

constraints: Exactly one word has a different step pattern from the others
hints: Turn each word into its step pattern. Two words match if their patterns are equal.
Patterns are lists, so turn each into a string key such as "2,-1" and count keys in a hash map.
Alternatively: among the first three words, two must share the common pattern. Find it, then return the first word that does not match.

explain.intuition:
The words themselves can look completely different ("ace" and "moq") yet behave the same, because only the gaps matter. So reduce every word to a signature: its gaps joined into a string. Then the problem is "find the one signature that occurs once", a plain counting job.

A neat shortcut: with at least three words and only one odd, at least two of the first three share the common pattern. Take the majority of those three as the reference and return the word that differs from it.
steps: For each word build a key: the gaps word[j+1] − word[j] joined with commas.
Count how many words have each key.
Return the word whose key count is 1.
pitfalls: Comparing every word to the first one. If the first word is the odd one, every other word looks odd.
Joining gaps without a separator. The gaps [1, 12] and [11, 2] both become "112".
Using absolute gaps. "ab" steps +1 and "ba" steps −1; they are different patterns.

solutions.title: Count signatures
solutions.idea: Map each word to its gap signature, count signatures, and return the word whose signature is unique.

solutions.title: Majority of the first three
solutions.idea: Two of the first three words must share the common pattern. Use it as the reference and return the first word that differs.

followups: Two groups of words share patterns and you must return the smaller group. What changes?
Group a large list of words by step pattern, like grouping anagrams. Which key would you use?
